messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Arjun's Vigilance

Arjun was thirty-six years old when he first sat down in a therapist's office, though his face carried the exhaustion of someone much older. He had scheduled the appointment on a Friday afternoon, timing it so that he could leave work early without drawing questions from his colleagues at the accounting firm where he had worked for the past eleven years. Even that small deviation from routine—leaving before five o'clock—had required him to rehearse an excuse about a dental appointment, a lie he hated but felt necessary. He was the kind of man who did not call attention to himself, who arrived at the office at 7:45 a.m. and left at 5:30 p.m., who ate lunch at his desk, who had perfected the art of being present without being seen.

The trauma that had brought him to this moment had occurred thirty years earlier, in the basement apartment in Queens where he had lived with his parents and younger sister. Arjun was six years old. His father, a man whose moods shifted like weather, had come home drunk on a Saturday afternoon. What began as shouting escalated into something Arjun could not fully process then and still could not articulate now. His mother had tried to shield him and his sister, had pushed them toward the bedroom, but Arjun had frozen in the doorway, watching his father's face contort with rage, watching his mother's body crumple against the kitchen counter, watching the way she raised her arms not to fight but to protect her head. The sound—that particular sound of impact, of breaking glass, of his mother's cry—lived in his nervous system in a way that words could never capture. When he tried to explain it to the therapist, he found himself unable to do so. The memory would flood back complete and uncontrollable, but the words never came. It was as if his body remembered in a language his mind could not translate.

For decades, Arjun had believed that the incident was an isolated event, that he had moved past it. His parents had eventually divorced. His father had moved to California and largely disappeared from their lives. His mother had rebuilt herself with quiet dignity. Arjun had become successful—a CPA, financially stable, unremarkable in the way he had always wanted to be. Then he had married Priya, a woman he had loved genuinely, and for five years the marriage had been, he thought, good. But somewhere in the sixth year, something had shifted. He found himself monitoring Priya's moods with an intensity that frightened him. When she raised her voice during an argument—even a normal marital disagreement about finances or household tasks—his entire body would seize. His heart would race. His hands would shake. He would become certain that escalation was inevitable, that violence was imminent, that he was powerless to stop it. Priya had tried to understand at first. She had suggested therapy, had asked what was wrong, had held him when he woke gasping from nightmares. But his hypervigilance had metastasized into the relationship itself. He watched her face, her posture, the tone of her voice. He anticipated threats that did not exist. He found himself apologizing for things he had not done, agreeing to things he did not want, anything to maintain a precarious peace that could shatter at any moment.

The divorce had been finalized two years ago. Priya had been kind about it, had not contested anything, had simply withdrawn from a marriage that had become suffocating for them both. Arjun had told himself that he was relieved. Without a partner, there was no one to hurt. There was no one whose safety depended on his constant vigilance.

But the hypervigilance had not diminished. If anything, it had intensified. At work, he found himself unable to concentrate. His colleagues had begun to notice. Last month, his supervisor had pulled him aside and asked if everything was all right; apparently Arjun had made an error in a client's tax return, something that had never happened before in his eleven years at the firm. The mistake had haunted him for weeks. He had come to believe that he could not be trusted, that his mind was fundamentally compromised, that he was destined to fail at everything that mattered. His body remained in a constant state of readiness, muscles perpetually tense, sleep shallow and fractured. He had come to understand, with a certainty that felt like truth, that the people responsible for what had happened to him—his father, and in some way his mother for not protecting him from witnessing it—had never faced any real consequence. His father lived in San Diego with a second family. His mother had moved on. And Arjun remained trapped in that basement apartment, his six-year-old self forever frozen at the threshold, watching, unable to stop what was happening, unable to protect anyone, unable to protect himself.

What had finally driven him to make the appointment was a moment three weeks earlier. He had been sitting in the break room at work when a colleague had dropped a ceramic mug. The sound of it shattering against the tile floor had sent Arjun into a state of panic so acute that he had had to leave the building. He had driven home and sat in his apartment for hours, his body unable to settle, his mind replaying not the mug but the sound of glass breaking in his childhood kitchen, the sound of his mother's fear. He had realized then that he was no longer functioning. The person he used to be—the happy person, the person who could engage with the world without constant dread—had vanished so gradually that he could not identify the moment of his disappearance. All that remained was this vigilant, exhausted version, scanning always for danger, finding it everywhere, certain that nothing he did would ever be enough to prevent catastrophe.
